plain_english: People will admit some things about themselves, but not others. No one will admit they're stupid or lack understanding. Instead, you'll hear everyone say, "I wish my luck matched my brains." But people readily admit they're scared. They'll say, "I'm pretty timid, I admit it. But otherwise, you won't find me foolish." A man won't easily admit he lacks self-control. He definitely won't admit he's unfair. He won't admit he's jealous or a meddler. Most people will admit they're caring. So what's going on here?
original_excerpt: Some things men readily confess, and other things they do not. No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding. But men readily confess that they are timid, and they say: I am rather timid, I confess; but as to other respects you will not find me to be foolish. A man will not readily confess that he is intemperate; and that he is unjust, he will not confess at all. He will by no means confess that he is envious or a busybody. Most men will confess that they are compassionate. What then is the reason?

plain_english: The main problem is that people are confused and inconsistent about what's good and what's bad. Different people have different reasons for this. Usually, they won't admit to what they think is shameful. They think being timid shows good character. They think being overly sympathetic is also good. But they think being foolish is what slaves do. They won't admit to things that hurt society. But they will confess to most other mistakes. Why? Because they think these mistakes are involuntary — like timidity and too much sympathy. If someone admits they lack self-control, they blame it on passion. They say it's not their fault. But people don't think injustice is involuntary. They also think jealousy just happens to them involuntarily. So they'll confess to being jealous too.
original_excerpt: The chief thing (the ruling thing) is inconsistency and confusion in the things which relate to good and evil. But different men have different reasons; and generally what they imagine to be base, they do not confess at all. But they suppose timidity to be a characteristic of a good disposition, and compassion also; but silliness to be the absolute characteristic of a slave. And they do not at all admit (confess) the things which are offences against society. But in the case of most errors for this reason chiefly they are induced to confess them, because they imagine that there is something involuntary in them as in timidity and compassion; and if a man confess that he is in any respect intemperate, he alleges love (or passion) as an excuse for what is involuntary. But men do not imagine injustice to be at all involuntary. There is also in jealousy, as they suppose, something involuntary; and for this reason they confess to jealousy also.

plain_english: You live surrounded by people who are completely confused. They don't know what they're saying. They don't understand what problems they have or don't have, why they have them, or how to fix them. Given this situation, I think it's worth the effort to constantly watch yourself and ask: Am I one of them too? What do I imagine about myself? How do I actually behave? Do I act like a wise person? Do I act with self-control? Do I ever claim that I've been taught to handle whatever happens? Do I have the humility that someone who knows nothing should have — the awareness that I know nothing? When I go to my teacher, do I go like people go to oracles, ready to obey? Or do I go like some whining schoolboy just trying to learn facts and understand books I didn't get before, so I can maybe explain them to others later?
original_excerpt: Living then among such men, who are so confused, so ignorant of what they say, and of the evils which they have or have not, and why they have them, or how they shall be relieved of them, I think it is worth the trouble for a man to watch constantly (and to ask) whether I also am one of them, what imagination I have about myself, how I conduct myself, whether I conduct myself as a prudent man, whether I conduct myself as a temperate man, whether I ever say this, that I have been taught to be prepared for everything that may happen. Have I the consciousness, which a man who knows nothing ought to have, that I know nothing? Do I go to my teacher as men go to oracles, prepared to obey? or do I like a snivelling boy go to my school to learn history and understand the books which I did not understand before, and, if it should happen so, to explain them also to others?

plain_english: You got into a fight at home with some poor slave. You turned your whole household upside down. You scared the neighbors. Then you come to me acting like you're some wise person. You sit down and judge how I explained some word or how I rambled about whatever popped into my head. You show up full of jealousy and feeling small because you're bringing nothing from home. During our discussions, you're not thinking about anything except how your father feels about you and your brother. 'What are they saying about me back there? They probably think I'm getting better and saying, He'll come back knowing everything.' I wish I could learn it all before I go home. But it takes hard work. Nobody sends me anything. The baths here in Nicopolis are filthy. Everything's bad at home, and everything's bad here.
original_excerpt: Man, you have had a fight in the house with a poor slave, you have turned the family upside down, you have frightened the neighbors, and you come to me as if you were a wise man, and you take your seat and judge how I have explained some word, and how I have babbled whatever came into my head. You come full of envy, and humbled, because you bring nothing from home; and you sit during the discussion thinking of nothing else than how your father is disposed towards you and your brother. What are they saying about me there? now they think that I am improving, and are saying, He will return with all knowledge. I wish I could learn everything before I return; but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.
